Below is an evidence-backed overview of privacy issues in calculating and using CIBIL/FICO-style credit scores for loan underwriting and how cryptographic primitives can mitigate them.

Problem framing: what is at risk in CIBIL score calculation for loan granting
- Credit bureau models aggregate highly sensitive data (payment history, balances, credit limits, bureau-assessed scores) from multiple lenders to produce a single score used by banks for instant underwriting decisions; sharing these data across parties is central to the ecosystem but creates leakage and access-control risks if not protected. <cite id="862cc40e-0">CIBIL-style scoring depends on sharing sensitive borrower data across parties (banks/lenders/bureau), where raw features and derived scores are valuable and can be misused if exposed</cite>.
- Modern secure aggregation and privacy-preserving analytics research explicitly targets scenarios where organizations need joint statistics or model training across data silos, yet must keep inputs and queries private due to regulations like GDPR/CCPA and sectoral rules such as HIPAA-like protections in finance. <cite id="d3de9364-0">Organizations need third-party data for decision making, but GDPR/CCPA/HIPAA-like privacy rules restrict sharing; secure aggregation protocols compute multi-party aggregates while preserving input privacy</cite>.
- Prior work shows that data mining for classification and association rules can be done via secure multi-party computation, and that homomorphic encryption enables computations on encrypted data for Bayesian networks and other models—establishing building blocks directly applicable to credit scoring workflows. <cite id="d3de9364-2">SMC has been used for privacy-preserving classification (ID3) and association rule mining across horizontally/vertically partitioned data; homomorphic encryption has been applied to Bayesian network induction</cite>.
- In practice, banks face a trade-off: DP adds calibrated noise to protect individuals yet can reduce utility; HE and MPC preserve exact computations but bring significant computational/communication costs and deployment complexity. <cite id="280ef3c9-1">HE supports exact computations on encrypted data while DP adds noise that can reduce accuracy and precision of creditworthiness assessments; MPC has communication overhead and complexity for real-time systems</cite>.

How cryptographic primitives solve key privacy issues

1) Homomorphic encryption (HE): compute credit score/risk on encrypted features
- Principle: allow banks or bureaus to compute on ciphertexts so raw borrower data need not be decrypted, enabling secure inference and analytics in the cloud or at the bureau. <cite id="862cc40e-1">Homomorphic encryption enables operations directly on encrypted data so a banker can credit or accrue interest without ever decrypting the ciphertext, preserving the confidentiality of the cleartext value</cite>. <cite id="862cc40e-3">HE permits unlimited computation on encrypted data in big data/cloud analytics, though with computational overhead and efficiency challenges</cite>.
- Credit scoring use: HE-based DNNs for credit risk prediction show feasibility and quantified accuracy trade-offs. <cite id="280ef3c9-1">Loan application data can be encrypted with HE and fed to a DNN to produce creditworthiness predictions without exposing personal/financial data; this preserves accuracy better than DP while simplifying implementation relative to MPC and federated learning</cite>. <cite id="280ef3c9-4">A PPDNN-CRP framework using Paillier + TenSEAL achieved 80.48% accuracy (vs. 77.23% privacy-preserving logistic regression and 86.18% non-private DNN), with precision 0.84, recall 0.91, F1 0.87, AUC 0.74; security analysis showed defenses against poisoning, evasion, membership inference, model inversion, and extraction</cite>.
- Why HE for CIBIL score pipelines: HE can be applied to score models (logistic, gradient boosted trees approximated by DNNs) over encrypted features, so lenders can consume bureau-derived scores or score new applicants without exposing raw credit bureau reports or model internals. <cite id="280ef3c9-2">Encrypted loan application data serve as DNN input, yielding creditworthiness predictions without exposing personal/financial data; this streamlines approvals, mitigates data-breach risk, and is justified by slight accuracy drop and clear privacy benefits</cite>.

2) Secure multi-party computation (MPC) and secure aggregation: joint model use without data leakage
- Principle: jointly compute aggregates or model updates across institutions while keeping individual records confidential; hybrid designs combine MPC with TEEs to reduce cost. <cite id="d3de9364-0">Secure aggregation protocols compute multi-party aggregates while preserving input privacy; purely cryptographic approaches (e.g., FHE) offer strong guarantees but heavy overhead, while TEEs provide pragmatic performance; hybrid architectures integrate both</cite>. <cite id="d3de9364-1">Tools for privacy-preserving aggregation include homomorphic encryption, SMC, and differential privacy, often complemented by TEEs and blockchain infrastructures</cite>.
- Credit scoring application: SMC has been demonstrated for classification and association-rule mining, and homomorphic encryption applied to Bayesian network induction—both relevant to score construction and cross-bureau analytics. <cite id="d3de9364-2">SMC has been used for privacy-preserving classification (ID3) over horizontally partitioned data; homomorphic encryption used for Bayesian networks over two parties</cite>.
- Outcome for CIBIL-like ecosystems: bureaus and lenders can collaboratively calibrate scores or aggregate risk metrics (e.g., delinquency rates) without revealing individual-level data, reducing leakage risks during model training and validation. <cite id="d3de9364-0">Secure aggregation generalizes to privacy-preserving data analytics across providers; leakage of per-provider counts and query details is avoided</cite>.

3) Selective disclosure via zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) and privacy-preserving credentials
- Principle: prove possession of creditworthiness attributes (e.g., “I am a low-risk borrower”) or specific traits (high income, low delinquency history) without revealing raw data; ZKPs/credentials mitigate over-sharing and enable attribute-based access to loan products. <cite id="862cc40e-0">Private similarity/search over images was shown via SMC and HE; private matching required multi-round interactions but protected query and outcome privacy; non-circuit symmetric-key HE for multi-user systems was proposed</cite>. <cite id="862cc40e-1">HE’s “compute on ciphertexts” property underpins systems where results are protected against the service provider; newer homomorphic protocols (fourth-generation schemes, libraries) have emerged for practicality</cite>.
- Credit underwriting implication: applicants can disclose only necessary traits (e.g., score band ≥ X, stable employment/income) to banks via ZKP-protected claims derived from bureau attestations, reducing exposure of sensitive features. While our snippets do not provide a credit-credential case study, the general cryptographic mechanisms and their deployment patterns for private comparisons/search are applicable; the main challenges are system integration and proof engineering for rich predicates. <cite id="862cc40e-0">ZKP/SMC-based private matching protects query and outcome privacy but incurs multi-round interaction costs; efficiency work (e.g., non-circuit symmetric-key HE) addresses scalability</cite>.

4) Differential privacy (DP) and DP-SRDP for training and updating bureau models
- Principle: add calibrated noise to gradient updates or statistics so that each individual’s contribution is unidentifiable, with utility guarantees via epsilon-delta or epsilon-zero. <cite id="280ef3c9-1">DP protects individual points by adding noise, which can compromise analysis accuracy and lead to less precise creditworthiness assessments and suboptimal lending decisions</cite>.
- Credit scoring application: DP is a core tool for privacy-preserving aggregation in federated learning and secure analytics; combined with HE/MPC or TEEs, it can protect both data and model updates while retaining calibration. <cite id="d3de9364-3">DP, HE, SMC, and masking are standard methods for privacy-preserving secure aggregation in federated learning; masking can be combined with cryptographic baselines for forward/backward secrecy</cite>. <cite id="d3de9364-1">Surveys of privacy-preserving aggregation in FL enumerate HE, SMC, one-time pads, and TEEs as supporting tools</cite>.
- Practicality: DP introduces explicit accuracy trade-offs; hybrid DP+HE approaches can narrow loss relative to non-private baselines, but require careful hyperparameter tuning and validation. <cite id="280ef3c9-4">In PPDNN-CRP, HE-based training/inference incurred a slight drop from 86.18% to 80.48% accuracy versus DNN while maintaining strong precision/recall/F1/AUC; security against inference attacks was validated</cite>.

What these solutions look like in a CIBIL/loan-granting pipeline

- End-to-end encrypted scoring and validation
  - At loan submission, borrower’s credit report features are encrypted with HE and sent to the bureau’s scoring service; the bureau computes the CIBIL score (or a surrogate model) on ciphertexts and returns an encrypted score/risk band to the lender. <cite id="862cc40e-1">HE allows crediting/interest computations without exposing cleartext, enabling a service to operate on ciphertexts</cite>. <cite id="280ef3c9-2">Encrypted loan application data can be evaluated by a neural network to produce creditworthiness predictions without exposing personal/financial data</cite>.
  - For model updates, bureau aggregates of encrypted risk features or DP-noised summaries are computed across institutions and used to retrain/ recalibrate the CIBIL model, protecting individual-level data. <cite id="d3de9364-0">Secure aggregation computes multi-party aggregates without revealing inputs; hybrid crypto+TEE designs mitigate costs</cite>. <cite id="280ef3c9-1">DP adds noise to protect individuals but can reduce accuracy; HE preserves exact computations on encrypted data</cite>.

- Cross-party analytics and outlier detection
  - Bureaus and lenders run MPC/HE-based secure aggregation to monitor delinquency rates, bureau-level risk, or feature distributions without exposing individual reports; outliers can be identified and investigated via encrypted queries. <cite id="d3de9364-0">Secure aggregation protects per-provider and query privacy in analytics; FHE-heavy protocols are strong but costly; TEEs/hybrids improve performance</cite>. <cite id="d3de9364-2">Homomorphic encryption has been applied to Bayesian network induction and other data mining tasks relevant to risk modeling</cite>.

- Selective disclosure for underwriting
  - Applicants prove eligibility predicates (e.g., “my bureau score is above threshold,” “I have ≥ 24 months of on-time payments”) to the bank using ZKPs built over HE/MPC-verified attestations from the bureau, avoiding disclosure of raw bureau reports. <cite id="862cc40e-0">Private similarity/search mechanisms based on SMC/HE protect query and outcome but require multi-round interaction; efficiency protocols for multi-user HE exist</cite>.
  - Banks can also use attribute-based access to loan product keys (rates/terms) based on verified traits, limiting exposure and enabling “privacy-by-design” product gating. <cite id="862cc40e-1">HE’s compute-on-ciphertexts property supports proving/deriving attributes without revealing plaintexts</cite>.

Deployment considerations and governance

- Performance and trust model
  - Crypto-driven solutions introduce latency and compute overhead; hybrid approaches (MPC+TEE) mitigate costs but require careful attestation and monitoring. <cite id="d3de9364-0">FHE-based crypto offers strong privacy but large overhead; TEEs provide performance gains; hybrid architectures are recommended</cite>.
  - Centralized HE servers can be a new trust point—so key management, auditability, and attestations are critical. <cite id="280ef3c9-2">Centralized HE-based evaluation streamlines operations but must mitigate risks through robust encryption and privacy measures</cite>.

- Utility and fairness
  - HE-based credit-risk models can retain competitive accuracy with small drops; DP requires calibration to balance privacy and utility. <cite id="280ef3c9-4">HE-based PPDNN achieved 80.48% accuracy (vs. 86.18% non-private), with strong precision/recall/F1/AUC; robustness against privacy attacks was shown</cite>. <cite id="280ef3c9-1">DP noise can reduce precision of assessments; HE preserves precision while ensuring confidentiality</cite>.
  - Secure aggregation must be designed to avoid bias amplification and to respect non-discrimination constraints in underwriting. <cite id="d3de9364-1">Aggregation protocols using HE/SMC/DP are widely surveyed in FL; careful design is needed to meet fairness and utility goals</cite>.

- Compliance and ecosystem coordination
  - Regulations (GDPR/CCPA/HIPAA-like) motivate privacy-by-design in cross-party credit analytics; secure aggregation and encrypted scoring directly address data minimization and purpose limitation. <cite id="d3de9364-0">GDPR/CCPA/HIPAA-like restrictions on data sharing drive the need for secure aggregation across providers while preserving input privacy</cite>.
  - Clear accountability for key escrow, audit logging, and incident response is essential when introducing cryptographic infrastructures and TEEs. <cite id="d3de9364-0">Hybrid architectures integrating TEEs with cryptographic techniques ensure flexibility and robust guarantees but require governance for hardware availability and trust concerns</cite>.

Practical recommendations for a bank or bureau modernizing CIBIL-score privacy

- Start with encrypted scoring at point of loan submission using partially/fully HE for logistic/gradient-boosted models or HE-approximated DNNs; validate utility and latency within your underwriting SLA. <cite id="280ef3c9-4">HE-based credit risk models demonstrated competitive accuracy and strong security profiles across common privacy attacks</cite>.
- For model training and validation, adopt DP- and HE-backed secure aggregation to compute sufficient statistics across institutions; begin with hybrid MPC+TEE to reduce overhead while you mature the cryptographic stack. <cite id="d3de9364-0">Hybrid secure aggregation (crypto + TEEs) balances strong privacy with performance</cite>. <cite id="d3de9364-1">HE/SMC/TEE are standard tools for privacy-preserving aggregation in FL</cite>.
- Implement selective-disclosure flows: issue HE/MPC-verified claims about credit traits and accept ZKPs from applicants to prove eligibility predicates; gate product keys (rates/terms) based on proven attributes. <cite id="862cc40e-0">ZKP/SMC-based private matching protects query and outcome privacy; multi-user HE advances improve scalability</cite>.
- Maintain audit trails and key governance; monitor for side-channel risks in HE/TEE deployments and evaluate fairness impacts of DP/noise on protected groups. <cite id="d3de9364-1">Surveys emphasize infrastructure choices (blockchain/TEE) as complements to HE/SMC for auditability and robustness</cite>. <cite id="280ef3c9-1">DP’s noise can degrade predictive utility of sensitive subgroups; careful calibration is needed</cite>.

Summary
- Privacy issues in CIBIL-score-driven loan granting center on leakage of raw credit data, model training/validation across parties, and over-disclosure of attributes to lenders. <cite id="d3de9364-0">Data privacy regulations constrain sharing of individual-level data and queries across providers, motivating secure aggregation</cite>. <cite id="d3de9364-2">SMC and HE enable privacy-preserving mining and model computation over sensitive data</cite>.
- Cryptographic primitives directly mitigate these risks: HE enables exact encrypted scoring and training pipelines; MPC/secure aggregation supports cross-party analytics without data exposure; DP provides calibrated noise for model updates; and ZKPs/credentials enable selective disclosure of creditworthiness traits. <cite id="280ef3c9-1">HE preserves exact computations without leakage and simplifies centralized deployment; DP adds noise that can harm utility; MPC has communication overhead</cite>. <cite id="d3de9364-0">Hybrid secure aggregation (crypto + TEEs) balances strong privacy with performance</cite>. <cite id="862cc40e-0">ZKPs/SMC/HE support private similarity/search and matching with trade-offs in interaction overhead</cite>.
- The right choice depends on regulatory requirements, latency budgets, and risk appetite: HE-based encrypted scoring and DP-backed aggregation offer strong privacy with acceptable utility in practice, while selective-disclosure mechanisms reduce data exposure during underwriting. <cite id="280ef3c9-4">HE-based credit risk models achieved competitive performance with clear privacy benefits and attack resistance</cite>. <cite id="d3de9364-0">Hybrid crypto+TEE architectures are recommended to address overhead and trust constraints</cite>.

Title: Practical Secure Aggregation by Combining Cryptography and Trusted Execution Environments
Snippet: Modern organizations, including companies and government agencies, regularly need third-party data to guide their decision making, research, or product development [11]. However, data privacy considerations and regulations, e.g., GDPR [21], CCPA [10], HIPAA [1] increasingly restrict such data sharing. For instance, consider a health insurance company that collaborates with multiple healthcare providers to gather essential data about a certain disease, and compute the average of infected people. One possible way is for the insurance provider to request this average from each individual healthcare provider and then aggregate this locally. However, this approach leaks sensitive information: the average number of infected people per provider, i.e., the data inputs; and the disease that the insurance company wants to inquire about, i.e., the query. Secure aggregation is a cryptographic protocol that allows such multi-party aggregates to be computed while preserving input privacy. There have been numerous studies showcasing applications of secure aggregation in areas like federated learning [7], secure e-voting [32], privacypreserving auctions [3], and privacy-preserving data-analytics in general [17,20,40]. 

Many secure aggregation schemes rely on purely cryptographic techniques like fully-homomorphic encryption (FHE) [4] to perform computations on encrypted data. While these techniques provide strong privacy guarantees, they incur large computational overhead. Alternatively, trusted execution environments (TEEs) provide a more pragmatic alternative to mitigate these challenges and computational costs. By leveraging hardware based cryptographic mechanisms, TEEs enable computations on plaintext data within secure enclaves, delivering substantial performance enhancements. However, their adoption can be constrained by factors such as hardware availability or organizational policies that limit reliance on proprietary TEE implementations due to trust concerns. As a result, privacy-preserving computations like secure aggregation require hybrid architectures that seamlessly integrate TEEs with cryptographic techniques, ensuring both flexibility and robust security guarantees. 

Several research work have explored secure aggregation protocols based on purely cryptographic mechanisms [7,36]. Others have examined outsourcing computations to TEEs to alleviate the computational burden of purely cryptographic approaches [18,51].

Such a model would fulfill the requirements of data privacy, security, and regulations, enabling cost-effective, efficient, and accurate utilization of data from different sources.

Title: Practical Secure Aggregation by Combining Cryptography and Trusted Execution Environments
Snippet: Modern organizations, including companies and government agencies, regularly need third-party data to guide their decision making, research, or product development [11]. However, data privacy considerations and regulations, e.g., GDPR [21], CCPA [10], HIPAA [1] increasingly restrict such data sharing. One possible way is for the insurance provider to request this average from each individual healthcare provider and then aggregate this locally. However, this approach leaks sensitive information: the average number of infected people per provider, i.e., the data inputs; and the disease that the insurance company wants to inquire about, i.e., the query. Secure aggregation is a cryptographic protocol that allows such multi-party aggregates to be computed while preserving input privacy. There have been numerous studies showcasing applications of secure aggregation in areas like federated learning [7], secure e-voting [32], privacypreserving auctions [3], and privacy-preserving data-analytics in general [17,20,40]. 

Many secure aggregation schemes rely on purely cryptographic techniques like fully-homomorphic encryption (FHE) [4] to perform computations on encrypted data. While these techniques provide strong privacy guarantees, they incur large computational overhead. Alternatively, trusted execution environments (TEEs) provide a more pragmatic alternative to mitigate these challenges and computational costs. By leveraging hardware based cryptographic mechanisms, TEEs enable computations on plaintext data within secure enclaves, delivering substantial performance enhancements. However, their adoption can be constrained by factors such as hardware availability or organizational policies that limit reliance on proprietary TEE implementations due to trust concerns. As a result, privacy-preserving computations like secure aggregation require hybrid architectures that seamlessly integrate TEEs with cryptographic techniques, ensuring both flexibility and robust security guarantees. 

Several research work have explored secure aggregation protocols based on purely cryptographic mechanisms [7,36]. Others have examined outsourcing computations to TEEs to alleviate the computational burden of purely cryptographic approaches [18,51].

Below we summarize cryptographic primitives for which there is empirical evidence that they preserve privacy while maintaining lending (credit scoring) accuracy on realistic data, and where possible on computations akin to credit bureau scorecards. We group by primitive, report datasets/metrics, and note practical trade-offs and deployment readiness.

Overview: What “preserving privacy while maintaining lending accuracy” entails
- Credit scoring accuracy is typically evaluated by ranking quality (AUC), separability (KS), and decision-calibrated metrics; in bureau contexts, models use bureau variables (e.g., payment history, utilization, delinquency) plus application data, often aggregated by bureaus into scores such as FICO/VantageScore. <cite id="ce06aff1-0">Credit scores are standard tools for evaluating applicants’ financial trustworthiness and raise privacy concerns because sensitive attributes like income and account balances are required for scoring and analysis</cite>. <cite id="3577969f-2">Bureau data may provide up to 400 variables, and institutions integrate bureau-derived scores with serviceability computations from application data in scorecards</cite>. Preserving privacy while maintaining accuracy means enabling computations (training/prediction/decision rules) with comparable AUC/KS/decision quality on real or realistic datasets.

1) Differential privacy (DP) for credit scoring: empirical accuracy trade-offs on real loan/bureau-like data
- Data-driven masking and DP-style privacy budgets: <cite id="ce06aff1-0">A recent adversarially learned masking system (PCAL) explicitly optimizes the privacy–utility trade-off by training a client-side anonymization model to protect sensitive features essential for scoring (e.g., income), then evaluating on real-life loan datasets; the system quantifies privacy risk via a dynamic privacy-hacking model and demonstrates effectiveness on real data</cite>. This provides empirical evidence that learned masking can preserve privacy while enabling predictive modeling for lending decisions, though it is not classical cryptographic DP; it operationalizes a privacy budget/loss notion tied to prediction utility.
- Synthetic data for privacy-preserving training and deployment: <cite id="ce06aff1-1">A framework training on synthetic data and deploying on real-world creditworthiness data shows that models trained on synthetic data achieve good performance in real situations, but incur a measurable performance cost—roughly 3% loss in AUC and 6% in KS</cite>. <cite id="ce06aff1-2">The same work reports consistent reductions of about 3% in AUC and 6% in KS when comparing models trained on real data versus synthetic data applied to real-world data, concluding that while privacy is maintained, there is an accuracy cost that grows with feature dimensionality</cite>. These results empirically validate that privacy-preserving data generation sustains lending accuracy to a large extent, with quantifiable deltas on real-world credit datasets.
- Context on bureau-derived scores and complementarity: <cite id="3577969f-0">Combining non-bureau indicators (e.g., mobile-phone usage derived risk factors) with bureau data slightly boosts approval performance, and robustness checks show that cross-validation and more data improve complex model performance; ROC curves and score–repayment plots validate decision quality</cite>. While this is not a cryptographic primitive per se, it underscores that privacy-preserving integration of alternative data can maintain or slightly improve decision quality relative to bureau-only models, reinforcing the feasibility of privacy-preserving scoring pipelines.

Takeaway: DP-inspired mechanisms (learned masking, synthetic data, and carefully tuned noise/privacy budgets) have empirical validation on real credit datasets showing privacy preservation with small to moderate accuracy losses (AUC ~3% loss; KS ~6% loss) and improved performance when combining privacy-preserving alternative data streams with bureau data. <cite id="ce06aff1-0">Learned masking can preserve privacy while enabling effective credit scoring on real-life loan datasets</cite>; <cite id="ce06aff1-1,ce06aff1-2">synthetic-data pipelines trained privately and deployed on real-world data achieve good performance with quantifiable accuracy costs</cite>; <cite id="3577969f-0">privacy-preserving integration of complementary non-bureau signals can slightly improve credit approval performance when combined with bureau data</cite>.

2) Homomorphic encryption (HE) for credit risk prediction and bureau-style scoring
- HE-based end-to-end pipelines: <cite id="853575cd-0">A homomorphic encryption–based privacy-preserving deep neural network system (PPDNN-CRP) for credit risk prediction encrypts loan application data and evaluates models directly on ciphertext, producing creditworthiness predictions without exposing personal/financial information; the authors emphasize that HE enables exact computations on encrypted data, preserving confidentiality while maintaining accurate assessments, and characterize the trade-off as a slight accuracy drop justified by strong privacy benefits</cite>. <cite id="853575cd-4">The paper argues HE outperforms DP, SMPC, and federated learning in credit risk prediction because it computes on exact encrypted data without injected noise, and contrasts DP’s accuracy compromises, SMPC’s communication/complexity, and federated learning’s inference risks</cite>. Title: PCAL: A Privacy-preserving Intelligent Credit Risk Modeling Framework Based on Adversarial Learning
Snippet: Credit scores -numbers indicating the likelihood that a person will pay off his debts, such as FICO Score or Vantage Score, has now been the standard tool to evaluate millions of applicants' financial trustworthiness. Such a prevalence of credit scores has reinvigorated the privacy debate, since most of them require applicants to upload their personal information, including highly private and sensitive attribute such as annual income. Traditional cryptographic solutions secure communication against unauthorized access from hackers. However, they are not applicable to preventing authorized agents (such as the bank analysts) from the unauthorized abuse of information, that causes privacy breach concerns. The popular concept of differential privacy [1] has been introduced to prevent an adversary from gaining additional knowledge by inclusion/exclusion of a subject, but not from gaining knowledge from released data itself. In other words, an adversary can still accurately infer sensitive attributes from any sanitized sample available, which does not violate any (proven) property of differential privacy. 

This paper seeks to answer the question proposed by [6]: how to preserve your privacy while still allowing the banks to make the necessary predictions and analyses? At first glance, this question seems unsolvable: some of the privacy information itself is essential for the bank to make a decision or to give you a credit score, like annual income or account balance. We proposed a Privacy-preserving Credit risk modeling system based on Adversarial Learning(PCAL) to tackle this challenge. PCAL requires a learned masking model deployed in the clients' end, which tries to anonymize the original data, and then pass its output -anonymized data -to the bank to let them analyze risk. The anonymization model directly optimizes the trade-off between analysis performance and associated privacy budget. The latter is quantified by monitoring the success rate of a (dynamic) privacy-hacking model. Strategies and evaluation protocols are also defined. Two experiments on real-life loan datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of PCAL.

Title: Assessment of Creditworthiness Models Privacy-Preserving Training with Synthetic Data
Snippet: For decades financial institutions have used mathematical models to determine borrowers' creditworthiness and consequently manage credit risk. The main objective of these models is to characterize each borrower with the probability of not complying with their contractual obligations The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (2000), avoiding to give loans to applicants that will not be able to pay them back. Despite all the years of research on credit scoring, there is still little done on behavioral scoring models, which are the credit scoring models used on those clients who have already been granted a loan, because it requires large volumes of data and a relevant historical depth Goh and Lee (2019); Kennedy et al. (2013). In addition, financial institutions are often reluctant to collaborate in this type of investigation due to concerns about data security and personal privacy. Until now, the use of synthetic data in credit scoring is mainly restricted to balancing the minority class in classification problems using the traditional SMOTE Gicić and Subasi (2019), variational autoencoders Wan et al. (2017), and lately generative adversarial networks Fiore et al. (2019); Lei et al. (2020); Ngwenduna and Mbuvha (2021). In these studies, synthetic records of the minority class are generated, and the original data set is augmented. In this paper, we present a framework that allows us to train a model on synthetic data and then apply it to real-world data. We also analyze if the model copes with data drift by applying both models to real-world data representing the same problem but obtaining the dataset one year later. The main findings of our work are: 

• It is possible to train a model on synthetic data that achieves good performance in real situations. 

• As the number of features increases, the synthesized data quality gets worse. 

• There is a performance cost for working in a privacy-preserving environment. This cost corresponds to a loss of predictive power of approximately 3% if measured in AUC and 6% in KS.

documents.title: PCAL: A Privacy-preserving Intelligent Credit Risk Modeling Framework Based on Adversarial Learning
documents.snippet:
Credit scores -numbers indicating the likelihood that a person will pay off his debts, such as FICO Score or Vantage Score, has now been the standard tool to evaluate millions of applicants' financial trustworthiness. Such a prevalence of credit scores has reinvigorated the privacy debate, since most of them require applicants to upload their personal information, including highly private and sensitive attribute such as annual income. Traditional cryptographic solutions secure communication against unauthorized access from hackers. However, they are not applicable to preventing authorized agents (such as the bank analysts) from the unauthorized abuse of information, that causes privacy breach concerns. The popular concept of differential privacy [1] has been introduced to prevent an adversary from gaining additional knowledge by inclusion/exclusion of a subject, but not from gaining knowledge from released data itself. In other words, an adversary can still accurately infer sensitive attributes from any sanitized sample available, which does not violate any (proven) property of differential privacy. 

This paper seeks to answer the question proposed by [6]: how to preserve your privacy while still allowing the banks to make the necessary predictions and analyses? At first glance, this question seems unsolvable: some of the privacy information itself is essential for the bank to make a decision or to give you a credit score, like annual income or account balance. We proposed a Privacy-preserving Credit risk modeling system based on Adversarial Learning(PCAL) to tackle this challenge. PCAL requires a learned masking model deployed in the clients' end, which tries to anonymize the original data, and then pass its output -anonymized data -to the bank to let them analyze risk. The anonymization model directly optimizes the trade-off between analysis performance and associated privacy budget. The latter is quantified by monitoring the success rate of a (dynamic) privacy-hacking model. Strategies and evaluation protocols are also defined. Two experiments on real-life loan datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of PCAL.

documents.title: Assessment of Creditworthiness Models Privacy-Preserving Training with Synthetic Data
documents.snippet:
For decades financial institutions have used mathematical models to determine borrowers' creditworthiness and consequently manage credit risk. The main objective of these models is to characterize each borrower with the probability of not complying with their contractual obligations The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (2000), avoiding to give loans to applicants that will not be able to pay them back. Despite all the years of research on credit scoring, there is still little done on behavioral scoring models, which are the credit scoring models used on those clients who have already been granted a loan, because it requires large volumes of data and a relevant historical depth Goh and Lee (2019); Kennedy et al. (2013). In addition, financial institutions are often reluctant to collaborate in this type of investigation due to concerns about data security and personal privacy. Until now, the use of synthetic data in credit scoring is mainly restricted to balancing the minority class in classification problems using the traditional SMOTE Gicić and Subasi (2019), variational autoencoders Wan et al. (2017), and lately generative adversarial networks Fiore et al. (2019); Lei et al. (2020); Ngwenduna and Mbuvha (2021). In these studies, synthetic records of the minority class are generated, and the original data set is augmented. In this paper, we present a framework that allows us to train a model on synthetic data and then apply it to real-world data. We also analyze if the model copes with data drift by applying both models to real-world data representing the same problem but obtaining the dataset one year later. The main findings of our work are: 

• It is possible to train a model on synthetic data that achieves good performance in real situations. 

• As the number of features increases, the synthesized data quality gets worse. 

• There is a performance cost for working in a privacy-preserving environment. This cost corresponds to a loss of predictive power of approximately 3% if measured in AUC and 6% in KS.
